warmup.q: A follower keeps up by running the leader's SQL statements again, in the same order. Which statement is certain to leave the follower's data the same as the leader's?
options: INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (41, 500, 'duplicate', now())
UPDATE accounts SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 500 WHERE account_id = 7, when a reconnecting follower may be sent it twice
UPDATE payments SET status = 'failed' WHERE payment_id = 41
DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now() LIMIT 1000
warmup.why: Setting a fixed value on a row found by its key gives the same result on any server, even if it runs twice. now() reads the follower's own clock, which is later than the leader's. A relative update sent twice adds twice. LIMIT without ORDER BY deletes whichever 1,000 rows the scan meets first, which can differ between servers, and it uses now() too. Logs that carry row values avoid all three.

sections.h: Ship the statement: small, readable, and different on every server
sections.html:
Lesson 1 said the leader writes every change into a log that the followers apply. It didn't say what an entry contains. Real systems give three answers, and each fails in its own way.

The simplest answer is the statement itself. The leader runs UPDATE payments SET status = 'settled' WHERE batch_id = 42, writes those 58 bytes to the log, and every follower runs the same statement. One entry can change 80,000 rows, a person can read the log, and followers on other versions understand it as long as the SQL means the same thing there. MySQL replicated only this way until row-based logging arrived in 5.1.

It breaks because a statement is a small program, and each follower runs it somewhere else, later. Anything that depends on where or when it runs can come out different:

  • now() and random(). The follower evaluates them with its own clock and its own random generator. In this section's demo the follower runs each statement 350 ms after the leader, so every created_at is 350 ms later and every random reference differs.
  • Auto-increment ids under concurrency. Two sessions insert at once. The first takes id 7, the second id 8, but the second commits first. The log is in commit order, so the follower runs the second insert first and gives it id 7.
  • Statements whose result depends on row order. DELETE FROM payments WHERE merchant = 'm2' LIMIT 100 deletes whichever 100 rows the scan meets first, and a follower built from a dump stores its rows in a different physical order.
  • Relative changes that arrive twice. SET fee = fee + 30 is right once. If a reconnecting follower is sent the entry again (lesson 1's catch-up), it charges the fee again.
  • Triggers and functions with side effects, such as an audit trigger that stamps now() or a function that calls another service. They run again on every follower.

The leader can repair some of this by writing values into the log. MySQL's statement format records the source's timestamp with each statement, so its manual treats NOW() as safe, and it flags statements that use RAND(), UUID(), SYSDATE() or USER(), and updates with LIMIT, as unsafe. In STATEMENT format an unsafe statement only earns a warning; in MIXED format it is logged as rows. MySQL 8.0 also made interleaved auto-increment locking the default because row-based logging had become the default: that lock mode isn't safe for statement-based replication. The PostgreSQL manual warns about middleware that sends the same SQL to several servers, such as Pgpool-II: random(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and sequences "can have different values on different servers".

The other repair is to forbid nondeterminism. VoltDB replicates by running the same stored procedures on every replica, and requires them to be deterministic. You know this rule from Temporal: it rebuilds a workflow by replaying its history, so workflow code must decide the same way on every replay, and it reads time and randomness through Workflow.currentTimeMillis() and Workflow.randomUUID(), whose values the history records (the Encoding track's lesson on durable execution). Statement-based replication is the same idea for SQL, with nothing to enforce the rule. Without something that enforces it, don't use it.

try.title: One log of statements, one log of rows
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. The leader runs five statements and writes both logs. Follower S runs each statement 350 ms later on its own clock; follower R applies the row events. Then the tail of each log arrives a second time, as after a reconnect.
Read the statement log and the row log side by side. Which row-log entries came from statement 4?
Predict, then run with -Pargs='pin', where the leader writes its own now() and random values into each statement before logging it. Which difference goes away, and which one stays?

  statement copy    1 m1          1250   60 d850e0b3  1000360   <- differs

Statement 4 became two row entries, one per row it changed. The statement copy has its own references and timestamps, and paid the fee twice when statement 4 arrived again; the row copy is identical to the leader, resend and all. With pin, the statements carry '23c52a1a', 1000010 instead of random() and now(), so references and timestamps match, but the fee is still 60: pinning values doesn't make a relative update safe to repeat.

sections.h: Ship the WAL: exact bytes, tied to one version
sections.html:
PostgreSQL went the other way. It already writes every change to its write-ahead log (WAL) before it touches a data page, so that after a crash it can replay the log onto its pages (the Storage track's lesson on write-ahead logging and crash recovery). A standby is a server whose recovery never ends: it receives the primary's WAL as it is written and replays it onto an identical copy of the data files. Oracle Data Guard ships Oracle's redo log the same way.

A WAL record doesn't say what the SQL was. It says which bytes changed where. In this section's Try it, one INSERT into refunds writes four records: a heap insert into the first 8 KB page (block 0) of the table's file, an insert into a leaf page of the primary-key index, a row lock on the referenced payment (the foreign-key check takes it), and the commit. rel 1663/16386/17262 names the tablespace, the database and the table's file. There is no now() to evaluate and no id to choose: the primary did all of that, and the standby copies the results bit for bit, indexes included. Nothing can drift.

The price is that the log speaks the storage engine's private language. Page layouts, tuple headers and index formats may change between major versions, so a PostgreSQL 17 standby can't replay a PostgreSQL 18 primary's WAL. You can't upgrade by upgrading the standby first and failing over to it, the trick that would make an upgrade nearly free. All the nodes of a physical cluster move together, with pg_upgrade and a short outage, or through a logical copy (next section).

The WAL also describes everything on the server: every database, every index page, every page VACUUM cleaned. You can't ship one table, and nothing outside PostgreSQL can read it.

So physical replication is the right format for what lesson 1 asked of a follower: an exact copy, ready to take over. For anything else, it is the wrong one.

try.title: Read the WAL records of one INSERT
steps: Start the primary and its standby from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait (about 20 seconds the first time). Open psql on the primary: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the SQL below. The first INSERT only warms things up; the one you will read is the second. Copy the two LSNs it prints.

In a shell, decode the WAL between them, with your LSNs: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -u postgres primary bash -c 'pg_waldump -p $PGDATA/pg_wal -s 0/5003FD8 -e 0/5005D88'. Match each rel number to the file nodes the last query printed.

code.title: psql on the primary
code.html: INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 700, 'customer_request', now()); -- warms up: see the expect SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 750, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id; SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS after; SELECT oid AS course FROM pg_database WHERE datname = 'course'; SELECT pg_relation_filenode('refunds') AS refunds, pg_relation_filenode('refunds_pkey') AS refunds_pkey, pg_relation_filenode('payments') AS payments;

try.expect:
The second refund is id 8, between 0/5003FD8 and 0/5005D88 here. Its records (your LSNs, ids and file nodes differ):

rmgr: Heap2       len (rec/tot):     53/  7297, tx:          0, lsn: 0/05003FD8, prev 0/05003FB0, desc: PRUNE_ON_ACCESS , isCatalogRel: F, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/1255 blk 47 FPW
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):    111/   111, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005C78, prev 0/05003FD8, desc: INSERT off: 8, flags: 0x00, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/17262 blk 0
rmgr: Btree       len (rec/tot):     64/    64, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005CE8, prev 0/05005C78, desc: INSERT_LEAF off: 8, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/17274 blk 1
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):     54/    54, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005D28, prev 0/05005CE8, desc: LOCK xmax: 852, off: 3, infobits: [LOCK_ONLY, KEYSHR_LOCK], flags: 0x00, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/17226 blk 0
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):     34/    34, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005D60, prev 0/05005D28, desc: COMMIT 2026-11-08 06:04:53.554268 UTC

Here course was 16386, refunds 17262, refunds_pkey 17274 and payments 17226. Transaction 852 is the INSERT: the heap record puts the row at item 8 of the table's first page, the B-tree record adds its key to the index, the lock record is the foreign-key check marking payment 3's row with a key-share lock, and the commit makes it count. The four add up to 263 bytes, with no SQL and no now() in sight: the commit time is a value the primary already chose. The first line has tx: 0: it is cleanup of a system catalog page by another part of the server, a reminder that the WAL carries everything that happens on it. Decode from before the first INSERT instead and you also see FPW records (whole 8 KB pages, logged on the first change after a checkpoint, as the Storage track's lesson explained) and a Sequence record: the identity column logging 32 values ahead.

sections.h: Ship the rows: a logical log
sections.html:
Between the two sits the logical log, also called row-based. Each entry describes one row. An insert carries every column's new value, an update carries the row's key and its new values, a delete carries the key, and a commit marker closes each transaction. The leader computes every value once, and the log records results, never the SQL that produced them.

In this section's Try it, UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = amount_minor + 50 WHERE payment_id = 4 comes out of PostgreSQL's logical decoding as:

table public.refunds: UPDATE: refund_id[bigint]:9 payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:350 reason[text]:'duplicate' created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'

The + 50 is gone; the entry says the row now holds 350. Applying it twice still leaves 350. Lesson 1's catch-up can send a follower entries it already has, and a log of results makes that harmless. MongoDB built its oplog this way on purpose: its manual says every oplog operation is idempotent, so an update that adds to a balance is recorded with the resulting value, and an update of many documents becomes one oplog entry per document.

A row entry says nothing about pages, so it isn't tied to the storage format. A follower can run a newer major version or a different storage engine, and it can take only some tables. That opens two doors. Upgrades: start a logical copy on the new version, let it catch up, then move the application in minutes. And change data capture: other systems can read the same stream, which is how Debezium feeds database changes into Kafka (the Stream processing track's lesson on dual writes and change data capture).

MySQL keeps its binary log as a second log next to InnoDB's own redo log, and row-based has been its default format since 5.7. Changing binlog_format has been deprecated since MySQL 8.0, and the manual expects row-based to become the only format. PostgreSQL has no second log. With wal_level = logical, logical decoding reads the WAL and turns it into row changes through an output plugin: pgoutput feeds the built-in publications and subscriptions, and test_decoding prints text you can read.

Rows cost more in some places. One UPDATE of 80,000 rows is one statement but 80,000 row entries. The follower finds each row by its key, so in PostgreSQL a table without a primary key can't publish updates and deletes until you set a REPLICA IDENTITY. And PostgreSQL's logical stream carries no schema changes and, as of version 18, no sequence values (lesson 4 covers what 18 and 19 add).

try.title: Decode three changes into rows
steps: With the servers from the last Try it running, switch the primary to logical WAL and restart it: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c 'ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = logical', then docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml restart primary.

Open psql on the primary (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course) and run the session below. Before the last query, predict what the UPDATE's entry will say about amount_minor.

Put the server back: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c 'ALTER SYSTEM RESET wal_level' and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml restart primary. Dropping the slot first matters: a slot nobody reads keeps WAL on the primary forever (lesson 4).

code.title: psql on the primary
code.html: SHOW wal_level; SELECT slot_name FROM pg_create_logical_replication_slot('peek', 'test_decoding'); INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 300, 'duplicate', now()) RETURNING refund_id; UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = amount_minor + 50 WHERE payment_id = 4; DELETE FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 3 AND amount_minor = 750; -- the last Try it's refund SELECT lsn, xid, data FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes('peek', NULL, NULL); SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('peek');

try.expect:
wal_level is logical. Each transaction comes out between BEGIN and COMMIT, with one line per row (the wide column header is trimmed; your ids, xids and LSNs differ):

    lsn    | xid |  data
-----------+-----+-------------------------------------------------------------
 0/6000110 | 859 | BEGIN 859
 0/6000178 | 859 | table public.refunds: INSERT: refund_id[bigint]:9 payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:300 reason[text]:'duplicate' created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'
 0/6002228 | 859 | COMMIT 859
 0/6004270 | 860 | BEGIN 860
 0/6004270 | 860 | table public.refunds: UPDATE: refund_id[bigint]:9 payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:350 reason[text]:'duplicate' created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'
 0/6004318 | 860 | COMMIT 860
 0/6004318 | 861 | BEGIN 861
 0/6004318 | 861 | table public.refunds: DELETE: refund_id[bigint]:8
 0/60063B8 | 861 | COMMIT 861
(9 rows)

The INSERT carries every column, including the created_at that now() produced on the primary. The UPDATE carries the key and the result, 350. The DELETE carries only the key: refund 8, the last Try it's. get_changes consumes what it returns, so a second call prints nothing; pg_logical_slot_peek_changes would leave the changes in place.

sections.h: Triggers: a change log you build yourself
sections.html:
Sometimes the database's own log won't do. You need one table copied into another kind of database, filtered or reshaped, from a version with no logical decoding. Then you capture changes yourself. A row-level trigger on the table writes a change row into a log table on every insert, update and delete, in the same transaction as the change. A separate process reads the log table in order, applies the changes somewhere else and deletes what it has shipped. Slony-I replicated PostgreSQL this way, table by table, to several standbys (its site now says it hasn't been updated in years and points to PostgreSQL's built-in logical replication). Bucardo used triggers to copy between several databases in both directions.

It is a logical log written by hand. It carries row values (the Try it stores each row as JSON with to_jsonb(NEW)), so it keeps the logical log's advantages: you pick the tables, the shape and the destination. It costs more, and the cost lands inside every user transaction, because each write becomes two plus the trigger's own work. In the Try it, 20,000 inserts took 76 ms without the trigger and 191 ms with it. Triggers also miss what nobody wrote them for: a new table, a TRUNCATE (row-level triggers don't fire for it), a schema change.

The idea is alive in two places. Audit tables keep the log table as the product. And the transactional outbox has the application write an event row in the same transaction as its data, for a relay to publish to Kafka; the Stream processing track picks that up.

Statement Physical WAL Logical (row) Trigger
An entry says the SQL text bytes at a page and offset a row's key and values a row's values, your format
Follower ends up identical only if every statement is deterministic yes, bit for bit yes if the trigger is right
Versions must match no yes no no
Other systems can read it no no yes yes
An UPDATE of 80,000 rows 1 entry 80,000+ page records 80,000 entries 80,000 log rows, in the transaction

try.title: Capture changes with a trigger, and time what it costs
steps: With the servers running, pipe the script below into psql on the primary (save it as capture.sql in the labs folder): docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -T primary psql -U sfz -d course < capture.sql.
Before you run it: in the timed part, the first 20,000 inserts fire the trigger and the second 20,000 don't. How much slower do you expect the first batch to be?
When you're done with this lesson's Try-its, docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v removes both servers.

code.title: capture.sql
code.html: CREATE TABLE refunds_changes ( change_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, op text NOT NULL, refund_id bigint NOT NULL, row_data jsonb, changed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp() ); CREATE FUNCTION log_refund_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN INSERT INTO refunds_changes (op, refund_id) VALUES (TG_OP, OLD.refund_id); RETURN OLD; END IF; INSERT INTO refunds_changes (op, refund_id, row_data) VALUES (TG_OP, NEW.refund_id, to_jsonb(NEW)); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER refunds_capture AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON refunds FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_refund_change(); INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (5, 420, 'fraud', now()) RETURNING refund_id \gset UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = 400 WHERE refund_id = :refund_id; DELETE FROM refunds WHERE refund_id = :refund_id; SELECT change_id, op, refund_id, row_data FROM refunds_changes ORDER BY change_id; \timing on INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 6, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 20000); ALTER TABLE refunds DISABLE TRIGGER refunds_capture; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 6, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 20000); \timing off DROP TRIGGER refunds_capture ON refunds; DROP FUNCTION log_refund_change(); DROP TABLE refunds_changes; DELETE FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 6;

try.expect:
The log table holds the three changes, each with the row as JSON (your ids and times differ):

 change_id |   op   | refund_id |                                                           row_data
-----------+--------+-----------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
         1 | INSERT |        10 | {"reason": "fraud", "refund_id": 10, "created_at": "2026-11-08T06:05:29.475533+00:00", "payment_id": 5, "amount_minor": 420}
         2 | UPDATE |        10 | {"reason": "fraud", "refund_id": 10, "created_at": "2026-11-08T06:05:29.475533+00:00", "payment_id": 5, "amount_minor": 400}
         3 | DELETE |        10 |
(3 rows)

Timing is on.
INSERT 0 20000
Time: 190.586 ms
ALTER TABLE
Time: 0.433 ms
INSERT 0 20000
Time: 75.503 ms
Timing is off.

With the trigger the batch took about 2.5 times as long. Running the two batches in the other order gave the same ratio (73 ms without, 187 ms with), so it isn't a warm-up effect. Your times depend on the machine; the ratio is the point, and every extra millisecond was spent inside the inserting transaction.

analogy: Three ways to keep a second set of accounting books in step with yours. Statement: phone the other clerk the instruction ("add this month's interest to every savings account") and let him work it out with his own calculator and today's date. Physical: fax him a copy of each page you changed, which only works if his book has exactly your page layout. Logical: send him each changed account line with its new balance. The first is shortest and drifts, the second is exact and brittle, the third is exact and portable, which is why most systems ended up there. The analogy breaks at speed and order: real logs arrive as a stream in strict sequence, and the clerk never gets to skip a line or ask what you meant.
world: Oracle has the same three layers. Data Guard ships redo, Oracle's physical log, so a standby must match the primary's version. GoldenGate and Debezium's Oracle connector (through LogMiner) read that redo and turn it into row changes, which is how Oracle data reaches Kafka. Temporal enforces exactly the determinism that statement-based replication only hopes for: your workflow code is replayed against its history, so you already write it with Workflow.currentTimeMillis() instead of System.currentTimeMillis(). When you build a change feed for a payments table, prefer the database's logical stream (Debezium on PostgreSQL or MySQL) or an outbox table over a homemade trigger, and give every consumer an upsert by key, so that a replayed change is harmless, just as it is in the oplog.
mistake: Turning on PostgreSQL logical replication for a table without a primary key. The publication is created without an error and inserts replicate fine. The first UPDATE or DELETE on that table then fails on the primary, inside the application's transaction, with "cannot update table ... because it does not have a replica identity and publishes updates". It happens because a row entry must identify the row on the follower, and a table without a key gives it nothing to go on. The fix is a primary key (best), a unique index named with ALTER TABLE ... REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX, or REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, which logs the whole old row with every update and delete and makes the follower search for it: more WAL, and slow applies on big tables. Check every published table for a key before you create the publication.

compare.title: One UPDATE, two logs

a.label: Statement-based
a.title: what the follower receives
a.html: UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = amount_minor + 50 WHERE payment_id = 4; -- one entry, whatever the number of rows -- the follower evaluates it against its own data -- sent twice: amount_minor goes up by 100

b.label: Row-based (PostgreSQL logical decoding)
b.title: what test_decoding printed (one line, wrapped)
b.html:
BEGIN 860
table public.refunds: UPDATE: refund_id[bigint]:9
  payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:350
  reason[text]:'duplicate'
  created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'
COMMIT 860

-- one entry per changed row, with the results
-- sent twice: amount_minor is still 350

compare.note: The statement is shorter and describes the intent, and the follower has to recompute it, so its answer depends on the follower's data, clock and luck. The row entry is longer and describes only the outcome, so any follower that applies it ends up with the same row, any number of times. Most systems log rows, and keep statements, if at all, for cases where the leader can prove the statement is deterministic.

worked.title: Read a PostgreSQL change stream from Kotlin, safely

steps.say: Create a logical slot once. The slot remembers how far its reader has confirmed, and the primary keeps WAL from that point on.
steps.code: -- needs wal_level = logical SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('refunds_cdc', 'test_decoding');

steps.say: Poll with peek, which reads changes without consuming them, so a crash between reading and applying loses nothing. Logical decoding only emits committed transactions, in commit order.
steps.code: data class Change(val lsn: String, val xid: String, val data: String) fun peek(conn: java.sql.Connection, max: Int = 1_000): List<Change> = conn.prepareStatement( "SELECT lsn::text, xid::text, data FROM pg_logical_slot_peek_changes('refunds_cdc', NULL, ?)" ).use { ps -> ps.setInt(1, max) ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> buildList { while (rs.next()) add(Change(rs.getString(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getString(3))) } } }

steps.say: Apply each change by key, so a change seen twice is harmless: an upsert for inserts and updates, a delete for deletes. Parsing test_decoding's text is fine for a demo; production code uses pgoutput through a replication connection, or Debezium.
steps.code: -- in the target database, for each INSERT or UPDATE line INSERT INTO refunds_copy (refund_id, payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (:refund_id, :payment_id, :amount_minor, :reason, :created_at) ON CONFLICT (refund_id) DO UPDATE SET payment_id = EXCLUDED.payment_id, amount_minor = EXCLUDED.amount_minor, reason = EXCLUDED.reason, created_at = EXCLUDED.created_at; -- for each DELETE line DELETE FROM refunds_copy WHERE refund_id = :refund_id;

steps.say: Only after the target has committed, tell the slot how far you got. The primary may then recycle the WAL before that point. If you crash before this step, the next peek returns the same changes, and the upserts absorb them.
steps.code: SELECT pg_replication_slot_advance('refunds_cdc', :last_applied_lsn::pg_lsn);

steps.say: When the reader is retired, drop the slot. A slot nobody advances keeps every WAL file from its position until the primary's disk is full (lesson 4's mistake).

lab.title: Statement replay against row replay
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder; no Docker. All 21 fail, because the leader builds its row log with exercise 1. Read ReplicationLog.kt: Server.execute runs statements with the server's own clock, random generator, id counter and heap order, and Leader.run writes both logs.

Exercise 1, rowEvents(before, after): one event per changed row, in id order. Run RowEventsTest, then StatementReplayTest: it now passes, and each test is one way a statement replica drifts (its own now(), its own random(), a fee charged twice, a LIMIT that picks other rows, swapped ids).

Exercise 2, Server.applyRow: apply an event so that applying it twice changes nothing, and move nextId past every replicated id, so that a promoted follower doesn't hand out an id it holds (lesson 1's GitHub bug). RowReplayTest replays every drift case with rows.

Exercise 3, pin: replace now() and random() with the leader's values before logging, as MySQL does for NOW(). PinTest shows what that fixes and what it can't. Then ReplayPropertyTest runs 100 random workloads per property.
hints: rowEvents: walk (before.keys + after.keys).sorted() and compare before[id] with after[id]: only after is an insert, only before is a delete, both and different is an update.
applyRow: a when (event) that puts event.row for inserts and updates and removes the id for deletes; then if (event !is RowEvent.Deleted) nextId = maxOf(nextId, event.id + 1).
pin: only Statement.Insert has values to pin. Use statement.copy(ref = ..., createdAt = ...), calling on.randomRef() and on.now() only for the parts that are Ref.Random and Ts.Now.
A property test failure prints the seed, the workload size and the lag. Paste them into a plain test and print leader.rows and follower.rows side by side.

drill.title: Decode a change into row events
drill.prompt: From memory, write rowEvents(before, after): given the table before and after one statement (maps from id to row), return an Inserted, Updated or Deleted event for every changed row, in id order. Then say in one sentence why a follower applying these events twice ends up with the same table.

answer.html: fun rowEvents(before: Map<Long, Row>, after: Map<Long, Row>): List<RowEvent> = (before.keys + after.keys).sorted().mapNotNull { id -> val old = before[id] val new = after[id] when { old == null && new != null -> RowEvent.Inserted(new) old != null && new == null -> RowEvent.Deleted(id) old != null && new != null && old != new -> RowEvent.Updated(new) else -> null } } // Twice is harmless: each event says what the row IS (or that it is gone), never what to add to it.

recap: A replication log can carry statements, physical page changes (the WAL) or logical row changes. Each is a different answer to "what does a follower need to reproduce this write?"

Statement logs are small and readable, and they drift: now(), random(), auto-increment under concurrency, LIMIT without ORDER BY, repeated relative updates and triggers all come out differently on a follower. MySQL pins NOW() and flags the rest as unsafe.
WAL shipping copies the primary's bytes exactly, indexes included, and ties every node to the same major version and the whole server. It is the right format for a failover copy.

A logical log carries each row's key and resulting values, so applying it twice is harmless and followers can run other versions or other systems. MySQL's row binlog, PostgreSQL's logical decoding and MongoDB's idempotent oplog work this way.
Trigger-based capture is a logical log you write yourself: flexible, but it doubles the work inside every transaction and misses what the triggers don't cover.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why PostgreSQL needs both physical and logical replication, when "replication is just copying the changes". Explain what each one copies and when you'd use it.
explain.answer: Both copy the changes, but they describe them in different languages. Physical replication ships PostgreSQL's write-ahead log, which says which bytes on which page of which file changed. A standby replays that onto an identical copy of the files, so it ends up exact, indexes and all, and it's ready to take over at a failover. The catch is that the log is in PostgreSQL's private on-disk format: the standby must be the same major version, it gets every database on the server, and nothing else can read it. Logical replication decodes the same log into row changes: this row was inserted with these values, this key now has these values, this key was deleted. Rows don't depend on the page format, so the receiver can be a newer version, take only some tables, or not be PostgreSQL at all. That's what you use for upgrades with little downtime and for feeding other systems like Kafka. It costs more for big updates, one entry per row, needs a key on every table, and doesn't carry schema changes. So: physical for the copy you fail over to, logical for everything that needs to move data somewhere different.

deeper.html:
MySQL's row events have a knob for how much of the row they carry: binlog_row_image is FULL by default (every column, before and after), and MINIMAL logs only the key and the changed columns. Smaller binary logs, at the cost of consumers such as Debezium seeing less of each row.

PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adds logical replication of sequence values, which closes one of the gaps this lesson listed; check the final release notes before you rely on it. Schema changes still aren't replicated logically: tools apply DDL on both sides themselves.

State machine replication is the general idea behind making statements safe: if every replica starts in the same state and applies the same deterministic commands in the same order, they stay identical. VoltDB uses it for whole stored procedures. Raft and Paxos (the Consistency and consensus track) agree on the order of the commands; determinism is the application's side of the bargain. Temporal's replay is the same contract applied to one workflow.

MongoDB's oplog lives in the capped collection local.oplog.rs. Since MongoDB 5.0 you can't write to it by hand on a replica set. Its size, 5% of free disk by default, bounded between 990 MB and 50 GB, sets the oplog window from lesson 1: how long a secondary can be away and still catch up from its position.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6 describes the same three log formats, and points out that a logical log is also the natural input for change data capture, which this course picks up in the Stream processing track.
